terms.grammar: gerō with mōrem and the dative of the person
evidence: Ter. Ad. 3.3.77: ut homō est, ita mōrem gerās (Lewis & Short), s.v. homō
Plaut. Asin. 40: Fīat, gerātur mōs tibi.
terms.comment: “To carry out someone’s wish”; the passive gives the reply: gerātur mōs tibi, have it your way.

terms.gloss: fall in with someone’s wishes, humour, give way to, comply with
evidence: Plaut. Amph. 995: rēctē facit, animō quandō obsequitur suō
Cic. Tusc. 5.60: cum huic obsecūtus sīs, illī est repugnandum (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Animō obsequī, to indulge oneself, do as one pleases.

terms.gloss: be kind or indulgent to, humour; give oneself up to (+ dative)
evidence: Cic. Tusc. 4.42: ipsa sibi imbēcillitās indulget (Lewis & Short)
Liv. 9.43.19: indulgent cōnsulēs legiōnum ārdōrī (Lewis & Short)
Tac. Agr. 4: in hujus sinū indulgentiāque ēducātus (Lewis & Short)

phrases.english: All right, have it your way.

phrases.latin: amat: sapit; rēctē facit, animō quandō obsequitur suō
phrases.english: he’s in love: sensible fellow; he does right to follow his own inclination
brought up in her lap and in her fond care

sources: Lewis & Short: mos · Lewis & Short: gero · Lewis & Short: obsequor
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 101, 330.
